questions.stem: A patient on a usual dose of lisinopril develops a persistent dry cough. A second patient takes twice the prescribed dose of warfarin by mistake and develops a hematoma. Which classification is correct?

options.B: The cough is a medication error; the hematoma is an ADR
options.D: The cough is an ADR; the hematoma is an ADE but not an ADR
options.E: Neither is an adverse drug event

questions.explanation: An ADR occurs at normal doses in normal use (the cough); harm from an overdose is an ADE that the ADR definition excludes. A: Overdose is excluded from the ADR definition. B: The cough involved no error in the process. C: The cough involved no error. E: Both are injuries from drug use, so both are ADEs.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes type B (bizarre) from type A (augmented) adverse drug reactions?

options.A: Type B reactions are unpredictable from the drug's known pharmacology
options.C: Type B reactions are common but rarely fatal
options.D: Type B reactions resolve with dose reduction
options.E: Type B reactions only appear after drug withdrawal

questions.explanation: Type B reactions are qualitatively abnormal, unpredictable, and not dose-related; rare but with high mortality. B: Dose-dependence characterizes type A. C: Common but rarely fatal describes type A. D: Lowering the dose doesn't prevent type B; the drug must be stopped. E: Reactions on withdrawal are type E.

questions.stem: A patient taking a non-selective β-blocker for angina develops bronchospasm. Which change best prevents this toxicity while keeping the benefit?

options.A: Increase the dose to improve angina control
options.B: Add a second non-selective β-blocker at low dose
options.D: Give the drug by IV infusion

questions.explanation: Benefit (β1, heart) and toxicity (β2, airways) come from different receptor types, so functional selectivity separates them. A: A higher dose worsens β2 blockade. B: Still non-selective. D: The route doesn't change receptor selectivity. E: A muscarinic agonist would worsen bronchoconstriction.

questions.stem: A patient on long-term prednisone stops it abruptly and develops hypotension, weakness, and hyponatremia. How is this reaction classified, and how could it have been prevented?

options.A: Type A; by lowering the dose
options.B: Type B; by never giving the drug again
options.C: Type C; by limiting cumulative use
options.D: Type D; by avoiding the drug in pregnancy
options.E: Type E; by tapering the dose gradually

questions.explanation: Addisonian crisis after steroid withdrawal is an end-of-use (type E) reaction, avoided by tapering. A: Type A is an augmented effect during use. B: Type B is unpredictable and unrelated to stopping. C: Type C relates to cumulative long-term use (e.g., NSAID nephropathy). D: Type D is delayed (carcinogenesis, teratogenesis).

questions.stem: Clavulanic acid has little antibacterial effect alone, but it makes amoxicillin effective against β-lactamase–producing bacteria. Which type of pharmacodynamic interaction is this?
questions.explanation: In potentiation one drug has little or no effect alone yet increases the other's effect. A: Additive means E(A+B) = E(A) + E(B), both active. C: Antagonistic means one reduces the other (naloxone + morphine). D: Synergism needs both drugs active, with a combined effect above the sum (TMP-SMX). E: The lecture classifies it as a PD effect-modification example.

questions.stem: A patient on digoxin starts amiodarone, which displaces digoxin from plasma proteins and also reduces its excretion. What is the expected result?

options.A: Brief rise in free digoxin that settles without a dose change
options.B: Fall in total digoxin with free digoxin unchanged
options.C: Fall in free digoxin as more is excreted; dose must be raised
options.D: Lasting rise in free and total digoxin; dose must be reduced
options.E: Lasting rise in total digoxin only; free digoxin unchanged

questions.explanation: Displacement plus reduced excretion blocks the escape route, so free and total levels both rise and the dose must be adjusted. A: That's displacement alone (e.g., phenytoin): the extra free drug is cleared to a new steady state. B: That's the new steady state after displacement alone, not when excretion is also reduced. C: Excretion is reduced, not increased. E: Free (active) drug rises too.

questions.stem: A patient on lithium for bipolar disorder starts hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. A week later she has coarse tremor, confusion, and vomiting. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Thiazide inhibits lithium metabolism by CYP3A4
options.E: Pharmacodynamic synergism at the same receptor

questions.explanation: Thiazides (and NSAIDs) reduce renal lithium clearance → accumulation of a narrow-therapeutic-range drug. A: Lithium isn't metabolized by CYP enzymes. C: Lithium isn't protein-bound. D: Absorption is already near complete. E: The interaction is pharmacokinetic (excretion).

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with osteomyelitis receives IV vancomycin over 10 minutes. Soon after, she develops flushing and pruritus of the face, neck, and upper torso, with mild hypotension. IgE testing is negative. What is the best way to prevent this with future doses?

options.C: Switch to oral vancomycin for osteomyelitis
options.D: Increase the dose and lengthen the interval

questions.explanation: Vancomycin infusion reaction is non-IgE mast-cell histamine release linked to infusion rate (a rapid reaction); slowing the infusion (± antihistamine pretreatment) prevents it. A: It isn't a true allergy, so vancomycin can be continued. B: Epinephrine isn't preventive here. C: Oral vancomycin isn't absorbed and won't treat osteomyelitis. D: Larger doses given fast would worsen it.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman taking a combined oral contraceptive is started on rifampin for latent tuberculosis. Which advice is most appropriate?

options.A: No change needed; rifampin doesn't affect contraceptives
options.B: Stop the contraceptive during treatment, with no other precautions
options.C: Use an additional or alternative non-hormonal contraceptive method
options.E: Take the two drugs at least 2 hours apart

questions.explanation: Rifampin strongly induces CYP450, lowering estrogen/progestin levels and risking contraceptive failure (the effect lasts until induction wears off after stopping). A: The interaction is well established. B: Stopping without an alternative leaves her unprotected. D: A lower dose would make failure worse. E: The interaction is enzyme induction, not absorption, so spacing the doses doesn't help.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man on rifampicin needed a higher warfarin dose to keep his INR in range. Rifampicin is stopped and the warfarin dose is left unchanged. Two weeks later he has gum bleeding and a high INR. What explains this?

options.A: Enzyme levels fall after the inducer is stopped, so warfarin is cleared more slowly
options.B: Rifampicin had displaced warfarin from plasma proteins
options.C: Stopping rifampicin causes enzyme inhibition within hours
options.D: Pharmacodynamic tolerance to warfarin has worn off

questions.explanation: Induction is slow on, slow off: after the inducer is removed, enzyme levels fall over days to weeks, and a warfarin dose raised to overcome induction becomes too high. B: Displacement would raise free warfarin while on rifampicin, not after stopping it. C: Removing an inducer isn't enzyme inhibition, and the change is gradual. D: The higher dose was needed because of faster metabolism (PK), not receptor tolerance. E: Potentiation needs both drugs present; rifampicin is gone.
